subject: Svenska
title: Source criticism and non-fiction
sourceSummary: Distinguishing fact from opinion, recognising biased texts, and judging whether a source can be trusted — the basics before upper-secondary school builds on them.

questions.prompt: Which of these sentences is a FACT sentence (can be checked)?
questions.opener: A fact can be proven true or false. An opinion expresses someone's personal view.
choices: Football is the most fun sport there is.
The capital of Sweden is Stockholm.
Everyone should exercise at least an hour a day.
Winter is the best season.
questions.explanation: That Stockholm is the capital of Sweden can be checked and is objectively true. The other statements express taste and personal preference — they cannot be proven true or false.

questions.prompt: What should you check FIRST when judging whether an article online can be trusted?
questions.opener: Before you even read the content — what does the SENDER tell you?
choices: Whether the text has many pictures
Who wrote the text and which organisation is behind it
How long the text is
Whether the text is written in Swedish
questions.explanation: The sender (who wrote it and which organisation is behind it) matters a great deal for credibility — an unknown, anonymous site is more uncertain than an established news agency or authority.

questions.prompt: An article about a new dietary supplement is written by the company that sells it. What should you keep in mind?
questions.opener: Who benefits from you believing the claims in the text?
choices: The article is automatically false
The company has a financial interest in presenting the product positively, so the text should be scrutinised extra carefully
It doesn't matter who wrote it
Companies are never allowed to write about their own products
questions.explanation: A financial interest (the company sells the product) makes the text biased, not automatically false. You should compare it with independent sources before drawing conclusions.

questions.prompt: What is the position an argumentative text wants to convince the reader of called?
questions.opener: It's the text's main claim — the thing the arguments are meant to support.
choices: Source
Thesis
Summary
Anecdote
questions.explanation: The thesis is the text's main claim — the opinion or position that the rest of the text argues for using arguments and evidence.

questions.prompt: You find a news story on a site you've never heard of. What is a good first step?
questions.opener: A simple way to check credibility without being an expert.
choices: Share the news right away if it feels important
Search to see if other, well-known news sources report the same thing
Assume it's true because it's written down
Just check how many people have shared it
questions.explanation: If several independent, established sources report the same thing, that increases credibility. The number of shares says nothing about whether something is true — false news often spreads quickly.

questions.prompt: "Studies show that 68% of students sleep less than eight hours a night, which is worrying." Which part of the sentence is an opinion?
questions.opener: One part of the sentence is measurable statistics, another part is a value-laden word.
choices: "sleep less than eight hours"
"which is worrying"
The whole sentence is fact
questions.explanation: The figure and the amount of sleep are measurable facts. "Worrying" is a value-laden word that expresses the writer's judgement — it's the opinion in the sentence.

questions.prompt: You are writing about climate change for a school assignment and find three sources: (A) a blog with no author given, (B) a report from a national weather agency, (C) a social media post with no source citation. Rank the sources by credibility and justify your ranking.
questions.opener: Ask of each source: who is the sender, and can the claims be checked?
questions.answer: 1. The weather agency report (B) — an authority with expert knowledge and a responsibility for accuracy. 2. The blog (A) — an unknown sender makes it hard to judge, but it might contain links to better sources. 3. The social media post (C) — least credible, with no sender or source citation.
steps: Source B (the weather agency): a government authority with expertise specifically in climate and weather — high credibility, often possible to verify against other authorities.

Source A (the blog): with no author given, you don't know who is behind it or what expertise they have — it must be scrutinised more, for example by checking whether it links to its own verifiable sources.
Source C (social media): with no source citation or sender, this is the weakest source — easiest for incorrect information to spread uncontrolled.
Conclusion: a good essay should primarily be based on B, possibly supplemented with A if it turns out to have good underlying sources, and should avoid building arguments solely on C.

questions.prompt: What four questions should you ask yourself when critically examining a text as a source?
questions.opener: Four basic questions before you trust a source.
questions.answer: Who is the sender, and what expertise/purpose do they have? Is the content fact or opinion — can it be checked? When was it published, and could the information be outdated? Are there independent sources saying the same thing? Be extra careful when the sender has a financial or political interest in you believing a particular message.
